abstract.title: Summary
abstract.p: Immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS)‐associated cognitive impairment is common in patients who receive chimeric antigen receptor T‐cell (CAR‐T) therapy. This study evaluated the utility of the clock drawing task (CDT) in detecting ICANS in patients with haematological cancers following CAR‐T therapy. Data were collected from CAR‐T patients at The Alfred Hospital, Melbourne, Australia. Patients underwent frequent assessments using the immune effector cell‐associated encephalopathy (ICE) score and the CDT, scored using a modified CLOX (CLOX‐M) rating scale, during their admission. We retrospectively reviewed the medical records of consecutive patients who received CAR‐T therapy between September 2022 and February 2024 to assess for ICANS and changes in ICE score and CLOX‐M. A total of 1208 clock drawings were time matched within an hour of an ICE score for 54 patients (39% female, 64.36 ± 13.25 years). Fourteen (26%) patients developed ICANS. Change in CLOX‐M scores from baseline and ICE scores was significantly correlated (ρ = 0.34, p < 0.001). Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis demonstrated that the CLOX‐M score has moderate discriminatory power (Area Under the Curve [AUC] = 0.737). A decrease in CLOX‐M score of 2 or more had high specificity (0.994) but low sensitivity (0.263) for detecting ICANS. The CDT can be used to complement the ICE score to improve ICANS monitoring.

sec.p: Keywords: chimeric antigen receptor T‐cell (CAR‐T) therapy, cognition, ICANS, immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome, neurotoxicity

sec.title: INTRODUCTION
sec.p: Chimeric antigen receptor T‐cell (CAR‐T) therapy has emerged as a promising treatment for haematological cancers including B acute lymphoblastic leukaemia, non‐Hodgkin lymphoma and multiple myeloma. 1 Its notable efficacy is owed to its specificity towards malignant cells. This is achieved by genetically modifying the patient's T cells to express specific synthetic chimeric antigen receptors, typically CD‐19 or B‐cell maturation antigen (BCMA)‐direct chimeric antigen receptors, which allows the T cells to target specific antigens on malignant cells. 1 , 2 Despite revolutionising the treatment of haematological malignancies, CAR‐T therapy is associated with adverse effects, including immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome (ICANS). 3 ICANS occurs in up to 67% 4 of patients following CAR‐T therapy. It typically manifests as a constellation of symptoms including headache, tremor and cognitive function, but can also progress to seizures, cerebral oedema and coma. Hence, there is a clear need for accurate and efficient recognition of ICANS to allow for better treatment and patient management.

The current American Society for Transplantation and Cellular Therapy (ASTCT) consensus grading system rates ICANS severity on a four‐grade scale using physical examination (i.e. level of consciousness, presence of seizures, motor findings and intracranial pressure/cerebral oedema) and the immune effector cell‐associated encephalopathy (ICE) score. 5 The ICE score ranges from 0 to 10 and is derived from the following: (1) orientation to month, year, hospital and city; (2) naming of three objects; (3) sentence writing; (4) attention (counting backwards from 100 by 10); and (5) language comprehension (the ability to follow a simple command). 5 While the ICE score is easily administered, it has been criticised for lacking the sensitivity required to detect changes in cognition following CAR‐T therapy. 6 The ICE score items are relatively ‘simple’ and not cognitively demanding, so it may not detect mild ICANS unless there is significant neurological/neuropsychological deterioration. This has encouraged clinicians to utilise or devise other cognitive screening measures to monitor cognition, such as the Montreal Cognitive Assessment, 7 the ability to follow multi‐step commands, 6 and other cognitive tests. 8

The clock drawing task (CDT) may be a valuable supplemental measure to the ICE score. The CDT reflects deficits across various cognitive functions including semantic memory, visuospatial function and executive function, which are currently not covered by the ICE score. Assessing executive function is particularly important, as it has been shown to be disrupted in patients with ICANS. 7 , 9 , 10 Certain responses during clock drawing may indicate executive dysfunction, particularly poor planning, organisation and self‐monitoring; for example, (1) drawing a too small circle; (2) unevenly distributing the numbers around the circle; (3) not writing the numbers in sequential order or not using numbered anchors (12, 3, 6, 9); (4) inability to self‐correct any errors that might be made; and (5) inability to recall the instructions or time asked to be drawn. In addition, the CDT is well accepted by patients and clinicians, so it is well suited for frequent serial bedside assessments required in the acute CAR‐T therapy setting. To date, the CDT has been found to be effective in detecting cognitive impairments and predicting outcomes in various populations including dementia, 11 multiple sclerosis, 12 , 13 traumatic brain injury 14 and stroke. 15 To the authors' knowledge, the CDT has yet to be used as a measure of CAR‐T‐related neurotoxicity. This study aimed to evaluate the utility of the CDT in monitoring ICANS‐related cognitive deficits following CAR‐T therapy, and hence, whether it can be used as a supplement to the ICE score.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: Fifty‐eight patients with haematological cancers were treated with CAR‐T therapy between September 2022 and February 2024 at The Alfred Hospital, Melbourne, Australia. In total, 54 patients were included in this study; one participant did not receive the full dose of CAR‐T therapy, one participant was unable to complete the CDT due to visual impairment, and two participants did not have available clock drawings in medical records.

sec.title: Ethics approval statement
sec.p: This study was approved by the Alfred Health Human Research Ethics Committee (HREC 219/23). Patients provided written or verbal informed consent, with a waiver of consent for medical record access for retrospectively recruited cases.

sec.title: ICE scores
sec.p: The ICE score was administered daily, and up to hourly, by the nursing staff and/or treating medical team. The frequency of administration was determined by the treating medical team based on the patient's neurocognitive status. The ICE score ranges from 0 to 10, with a score less than 10 indicating ICANS. 5

sec.title: Worst ICANS grade
sec.p: Medical records were retrospectively reviewed to determine participants' worst ICANS grade, as defined by the ASTCT Consensus Grading. 5 Medical records were independently reviewed by a CAR‐T neuropsychology fellow (C.K.) and CAR‐T neurology fellow (M.W.). Inter‐rater agreement was 100%.

There were six patients who scored ICE = 9 on a single occasion, and after further assessment of their records, their presentation was deemed to be inconsistent with ICANS. Potential explanations of these one‐point losses in ICE score included high‐grade CRS or environmental factors such as tiredness due to being wakened for an ICE assessment during the night. In all these instances, the one‐point drop in ICE score was transient, and the subsequent ICE scores were normal (i.e. equal to 10).

sec.title: Clock drawing task
sec.p: The CDT was administered following the ICE score. Participants were asked to draw a clock and set the hands to various times. Medical and nursing staff chose different times to set to reduce practice effects. The CDT was scored retrospectively using a modified version of the CLOX criteria 16 (see Table S1). Modifications included: (1) removal of the anchoring item, (2) modification of the hour hand item to accommodate different times and (3) modification of the last item to accommodate different minute hand intrusions and remove intrusion from circle criteria. This modified score will be referred to as CLOX‐M in the remainder of this study. Change in CLOX‐M score—henceforth, called ΔCLOX‐M—was calculated by subtracting the patient's first/baseline CLOX‐M score from their current score.

Clock drawings and ICE scores were retrieved from medical records from the patient's admission up to Day+30 post‐infusion; 2323 clock drawings and 2295 ICE scores were administered. Occasionally, patients declined or refused to be assessed using one measure, which may explain the mismatched number of clock drawing and ICE tests. In total, 1208 clock drawings were time‐matched within 1 h of ICE score administration (see Figure S1). Clock drawings were scored by a CAR‐T neuropsychology fellow (C.K.). One hundred and seventeen (10%) of the clock drawings were independently scored by a second rater, a CAR‐T Clinical Nurse Consultant (T.S.). Inter‐rater agreement was 94.87%.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: Analyses were performed in R (version 4.4.0). Spearman's correlation was used to examine the relationship between ΔCLOX‐M and ICE scores. To test our hypotheses, two primary sets of models were considered. All models included random intercept terms for patients to account for within‐patient correlations over time. In the first set, the association between ΔCLOX‐M (outcome) and its change over time, as moderated by ICANS status (‘yes’/‘no’; predictors), was evaluated. In the second set, the association between ΔCLOX‐M (outcome) and its change over time, as moderated by ICE score (score of 0–10; predictors), were investigated. In this second set, modelling was performed separately in subgroups of those who did and did not develop ICANS during admission. Models were constructed in a hierarchical manner to determine the best‐fitting model. First, interaction terms between ICANS/ICE score and non‐linear ΔCLOX‐M trajectories were examined by specifying restricted cubic spline terms (4 df) for time and the fit of the model containing the non‐linear ‘effect’ compared, using a likelihood ratio test, to a model containing a linear term for time. Second, the fit of the model containing the interaction term was compared, using a likelihood ratio test, to a model containing additive effects only for time and ICANS/ICE score. Furthermore, we generated receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves (using the cutpointr package) to assess the diagnostic accuracy of ΔCLOX‐M score in differentiating between ICANS (defined as ICE score <10) and no ICANS (defined as ICE score = 10). Finally, generalised linear mixed effects models were generated to investigate whether making an error on each CLOX‐M scoring item increases the odds of having ICANS (defined as ICE score <10).

sec.title: Descriptive statistics
sec.p: Fifty‐four patients (39% female, 64.36 ± 13.25 years, 12.18 ± 3.02 years of education) received CAR‐T therapy at our institution between September 2022 and February 2024 and had CDT and ICE scores available on their records. Of the 54 patients, 14 (26%) developed ICANS. Further demographic information is presented in Table 1. An example of ICE scores and CDT is shown in Figure 1.

sec.title: Relationship between ΔCLOX‐M score and ICE score
sec.p: Spearman's correlation demonstrated a significant positive correlation between ΔCLOX‐M and ICE score (ρ = 0.34, p < 0.001).

sec.title: Relationship between ΔCLOX‐M score trajectory and whether the patient developed ICANS
sec.p: The best‐fitting model contained a non‐linear effect for time and a significant interaction between time and whether a patient develops ICANS during their admission (see Table 2). Figure 2 illustrates that the trajectory of ΔCLOX‐M scores is relatively stable in the group of patients who did not develop ICANS whereas the trajectory of ΔCLOX‐M scores varies for those that develop ICANS.

sec.p: Further analyses comparing predicted ΔCLOX‐M scores at 5‐day intervals demonstrated that the ICANS group had significantly lower ΔCLOX‐M scores than the no ICANS group at Day+5 (predicted difference = −0.657, p = 0.012) and Day+10 (predicted difference = −0.632, p = 0.012) post‐CAR‐T therapy. There was no significant difference in predicted ΔCLOX‐M scores at Day+0 and Day+15 to Day+30.

sec.title: Relationship between ΔCLOX‐M score trajectory and ICE (stratified by ICANS status)
sec.p: Figure 3 depicts trajectory plots of ICE and ΔCLOX‐M scores across time stratified by patients who did (i.e. ICANS group) and did not develop ICANS (i.e. no ICANS group).

caption.p: Plots of ICE and ΔCLOX‐M scores across time for the ICANS and no ICANS groups. CAR‐T, chimeric antigen receptor T‐cell; CLOX, modified CLOX; ICANS, immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome.

sec.p: For the no ICANS group, the best‐fitting model contained a linear term for time, with no moderation effect of ICE score on ΔCLOX‐M trajectory. For those patients who developed ICANS, the best‐fitting model contained a linear term for time, but a moderation effect of ICE score on ΔCLOX‐M trajectory was now observed. Both ICE score (B = 1.870, 95% confidence interval [CI, 1.540, 2.199], p < 0.001) and time were significant predictors (B = 0.613, 95% CI [0.236, 0.989], p = 0.001), demonstrating that lower ICE scores and shorter durations since CAR‐T infusion were associated with worsened CLOX‐M scores. The interaction was also significant (B = −0.062, 95% CI [−0.101, −0.022], p = 0.002), such that the effect of ICE score on ΔCLOX‐M diminished as time since CAR‐T infusion increased.

sec.title: ROC curves
sec.p: The ROC analysis with bootstrapping with 2000 resamples demonstrated that ΔCLOX‐M score has moderate discriminatory power (Area Under the Curve [AUC] = 0.737, 95% CI [0.695, 0.779]) to detect ICANS (defined as ICE score <10). The ROC curve is depicted in Figure 4. At a cut‐off score of −2, accuracy was maximised (accuracy = 0.877) with high specificity (0.994) but low sensitivity (0.263). Positive predictive value was 89.5% and negative predictive value was 87.6%. The positive likelihood ratio was 44.56 and the negative likelihood ratio was 0.74.

caption.p: ROC curve of ΔCLOX‐M scores to detect ICANS (defined at ICE <10). CLOX, modified CLOX; ICANS, immune effector cell‐associated neurotoxicity syndrome; ICE, immune effector cell‐associated encephalopathy; ROC, receiver operating characteristic.

sec.title: CLOX‐M score error analysis
sec.p: Clock drawings were divided into two groups based on the ICE score: ICE = 10 indicating no ICANS and ICE <10 indicating ICANS. The frequency of CLOX‐M item errors was compared between these two groups (see Table 3). CLOX‐M item 1 (‘Does the figure resemble a clock?’), CLOX‐M item 2 (‘Is the outer circle present?’), CLOX‐M item 6 (‘Only Arabic numerals present?’) and CLOX‐M item 9 (‘Only two hands present?’) have complete separation. Generalised linear mixed effects models were conducted for all other CLOX‐M items, and this demonstrated that patients who make errors on most CLOX‐M scoring items are more likely to have ICANS (p < 0.001). The CLOX‐M items in descending order from largest odds ratio to smallest are items 14, 11, 12, 5, 3, 8, 10 and 13. Note, however, that CLOX‐M item 5 (‘Spacing intact along 6–12 axis?’) is scored out of two; two points for correct spacing and a point if there were errors in spacing that were corrected. Spacing errors (score of 0) on item 5 is significantly associated with ICANS, while self‐corrected spacing (score of 1) is not significantly associated with ICE scores. CLOX‐M item 4 (‘All numbers inside the circle?’) is not significantly associated with ICE scores.

sec.title: DISCUSSION
sec.p: Given the expanding use of CAR‐T therapy, there is a need for tools to efficiently diagnose and monitor ICANS. The ICE score is considered crude, so mild neurocognitive change may be overlooked, 6 , 17 and ICANS diagnosis may be delayed if the score is used in isolation. At this time, ICANS is currently defined using the ICE score, and hence, it is not possible to explore whether there are tools that are more sensitive to ICANS compared to the ICE score. Future research into cellular, serological and imaging biomarkers may be helpful in this respect. Rather, this study examined the use of the CDT, scored using the ΔCLOX‐M, as a potential adjunct ICANS assessment tool by evaluating construct validity. That is, does ΔCLOX‐M score worsen with the development of ICANS and improve with resolution, and thus, reflect ICANS‐related cognitive impairment. The CDT is a short 2‐min test that can be administered routinely by clinical staff of different skill sets (i.e. nursing staff, doctors and neuropsychologists) and, importantly, is well tolerated by patients. Results demonstrated that the ΔCLOX‐M score is associated with the ICE score and has moderate discriminative ability for ICANS when a cut‐off score of −2 (i.e. decrease in two points on CLOX‐M compared to baseline) is applied. The ΔCLOX‐M score demonstrated excellent specificity, low sensitivity, high positive and predictive values, high positive likelihood ratio and weak negative likelihood ratio. Clinicians can be confident that a positive test result (patient scores ≤−2 on ΔCLOX‐M) confirms the presence of ICANS. While a negative test result (patient scores >−2 on ΔCLOX‐M) suggests that the patient may not have ICANS, further assessment is needed. Hence, we suggest that there is a rationale for utilising both the CDT and ICE score. Changes in CLOX‐M score, when the ICE score remains 10, can prompt more frequent bedside assessments and observations to more readily capture a rapidly evolving ICANS. In cases when there is a mild ICE score change (e.g. 7–9/10) accompanied by an abnormal clock (e.g. case illustrated in Figure 1), clinicians may consider initiating glucocorticoids for Grade 1 ICANS over more conservative management and/or waiting for higher grade ICANS to initiate treatment.

Error analyses demonstrated that patients with ICANS were more likely to make errors across all CLOX‐M items except item 4 (‘All numbers inside the circle?’). However, we note that some patients deliberately wrote the numbers outside the circle, so this item reflected artistic choice rather than a lack of attention to detail or poor planning in our sample. The errors found in patients with ICANS likely reflect the underlying attentional dysfunction in patients with ICANS, rather than focal deficits (i.e. constructional apraxia, semantic knowledge breakdown) seen in other neurological conditions such as stroke and dementia.

The ICE score is the current gold standard to monitor for ICANS. 5 Mohn et al. advocated for greater involvement of neurologists in monitoring patients who received CAR‐T‐cell therapy, including the need for detailed baseline and daily examinations and the use of the Montreal Cognitive Assessment (MoCA). 7 We acknowledge that the level of neurology involvement proposed by Mohn et al. 7 may not be feasible in all hospitals. The MoCA typically takes 10 min to administer, and if performed multiple times a day, can be impractical to administer by nursing staff due to extensive time requirements. The CDT may be an alternative time‐efficient task compared to the MoCA; indeed, there is some evidence demonstrating a significant correlation between the CDT and the MoCA, albeit in other neurological populations and differing CDT scoring systems. 18 , 19

Some considerations need to be made when administering the CDT. The patient's generational (age), educational, language and cultural background are factors that have been consistently shown to influence performance on the CDT. 20 Pre‐existing cognitive impairment will also influence CDT performance. Hence, a comparison with the baseline clock drawing and the use of the ΔCLOX‐M score is most appropriate. Second, given repeated assessment, the time the patient is asked to set should vary to reduce practice effects. Nevertheless, given that the usage of a clock is relatively universal and relies less heavily on educational or language background compared to other cognitive measures, it is a practical measure for patients of differing backgrounds.

This study has several limitations. The CDT was administered prospectively, but the scoring with the CLOX‐M was done retrospectively. Given that the CDT was administered multiple times a day by nursing staff, it also relied on collation of other medical data for the day. The CDT and ICE score were completed on paper during a majority of this study's time period. While the day of assessment could be easily attained, 775 CDT and 316 ICE scores had incomplete timestamps. In addition, a 1‐h time‐matching criterion was used as ICANS typically evolves rapidly. This meant that not all CDT could be exactly matched to particular ICE scores. Second, there was some variability in the administration of the CDT among clinicians. For example, the level of difficulty of the time asked to set varied; some staff provided instructions that would elicit the ‘minute hand effect’ (i.e. difficulty setting the minute hand due to semantic knowledge breakdown; for example, drawing the minute hand to point to the 10 when asked to set ‘ten past five’) while others asked for ‘easier’ times (e.g. times on the hour, such as 3 o'clock). Additionally, the scoring procedure of the original CLOX was modified to accommodate this retrospective study, which may impact on validity. Third, our study cohort has relatively mild ICANS with only four patients with >Grade 2 ICANS, which is likely explained by the large proportion (44%) of patients with multiple myeloma. This limits the generalisability of the results. Finally, there is a potential population bias. Patients with high‐grade ICANS often cannot tolerate the CDT and so it was not administered. The decision to administer the CDT was based on clinical judgement. Despite these limitations, this study examined over 1000 clock drawings during the CAR‐T patient's admission and therefore provides important foundational steps for the utility of this practical score in this vulnerable and generally quite unwell population. Further studies using a prospective design to validate the CDT in the CAR‐T population are needed.

In conclusion, the results of this study highlight the potential utility of CDT to complement the ICE score in confirming ICANS. Future research is needed to explore and develop more sensitive measures of neurotoxicity. As the indications for CAR‐T therapy increase, cost‐effective and practical methods of monitoring for adverse effects—such as the CDT—are critical to improve recognition, diagnosis and management of ICANS. Ultimately, this can improve patient outcomes.
